parameters.name: image_size
parameters.description: Side of each frame.  The largest variant uses 384.

parameters.name: patch_size
parameters.description: Spatial side of a tubelet.

parameters.name: tubelet_size
parameters.description:
Frames a tubelet spans.  Sixteen frames become eight temporal
positions.

parameters.name: num_frames
parameters.description: Frames in a clip.

parameters.name: sampling_rate
parameters.description:
Stride, in original frames, between the frames of a clip.  Carried
because it defines what a clip is; nothing in the model reads it.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description: Channels per frame.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.description:
Classes the probe predicts.  Kinetics-400's count, since that is
the benchmark the paper leads with.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: The encoder, a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: The encoder, a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: num_heads
parameters.description: The encoder, a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: mlp_ratio
parameters.description: Feed-forward width as a multiple of `dim`.

parameters.name: layer_norm_eps
parameters.description: Epsilon of every LayerNorm.

parameters.name: uniform_power
parameters.description:
How the position table splits its width between time, row and
column.  `True` gives each axis an equal share, which is what
every released configuration sets; the code's own default is
`False`, which would give time half the width and the spatial
axes a quarter each.  Getting this wrong loads released weights
onto positions they were not trained with.

parameters.name: predictor_dim
parameters.description: Predictor width, for every variant.

parameters.name: predictor_depth
parameters.description: Predictor blocks, for every variant.

parameters.name: predictor_heads
parameters.description:
Heads inside the predictor.  `None` takes the encoder's count,
as the released code does — 16 heads across 384 channels, so 24
per head.

parameters.name: short_range_blocks
parameters.description: Blocks in the first mask collection.

parameters.name: short_range_scale
parameters.description:
Fraction of a frame each of those blocks covers.  The paper fixes
it rather than sampling a range.

parameters.name: long_range_blocks
parameters.description: Blocks in the second collection.

parameters.name: long_range_scale
parameters.description: Fraction of a frame each of those covers.

parameters.name: aspect_ratio
parameters.description: Aspect-ratio range, shared by both collections.

parameters.name: ema
parameters.description:
Momentum of the target encoder at the first and last step of the
*schedule*.

parameters.name: ema_schedule_scale
parameters.description:
How much longer the momentum schedule is than training.  The
released runs stretch it by a quarter and stop early, so the
momentum never actually reaches 1.

parameters.name: objective
parameters.description:
How predicted and target features are compared.  L1 is what both
the paper and the released code use — Section 3.1 says it was
found more stable than I-JEPA's regression.

parameters.name: smooth_l1_beta
parameters.description: Where smooth L1 turns from quadratic to linear, when chosen.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.vision.vjepa import VJEPAConfig
>>> config = VJEPAConfig()
>>> config.token_grid, config.num_tokens
((8, 14, 14), 1568)
>>> config.short_range_blocks, config.long_range_blocks
(8, 2)
Four times the pixels is four times the tokens:
>>> VJEPAConfig(image_size=384).num_tokens
4608
notes:
Reference: Bardes, Adrien, et al., *"Revisiting Feature Prediction for
Learning Visual Representations from Video"*, [arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471), 2024
— Table 6 for the variants and their results, Table 8 for the
architecture and the schedules, Section 3.2 for the masking.

members.summary: V-JEPA under the paper's attentive probe.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Frozen configuration; `num_classes` sizes the classifier.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.vjepa import (
...     VJEPAConfig, VJEPAForVideoClassification)
>>> config = VJEPAConfig(
...     image_size=32, patch_size=8, tubelet_size=2, num_frames=4,
...     dim=24, depth=1, num_heads=2, predictor_dim=12,
...     predictor_depth=1, num_classes=10)
>>> model = VJEPAForVideoClassification(config).eval()
>>> model(lucid.rand(2, 4, 3, 32, 32)).logits.shape
(2, 10)
notes:
Reference: Bardes et al., [arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471), Section 4.3.  The paper
evaluates a frozen backbone with this probe rather than with a linear
map on averaged tokens, and reports the gap at 17 points on
Kinetics-400 — so a linear probe compared against its tables would be
measuring something else.

Registered under `image-classification` because that is the task
this zoo has; the input is a clip rather than an image, which is what
the class name says.

members.summary: V-JEPA: a context encoder, an averaged target encoder, a predictor.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Frozen configuration.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.vjepa import VJEPAConfig, VJEPAModel
>>> config = VJEPAConfig(
...     image_size=32, patch_size=8, tubelet_size=2, num_frames=4,
...     dim=24, depth=1, num_heads=2, predictor_dim=12,
...     predictor_depth=1, short_range_blocks=2, long_range_blocks=1)
>>> model = VJEPAModel(config)
>>> out = model(lucid.rand(2, 4, 3, 32, 32))
>>> out.short_prediction.shape == out.short_target.shape
True
>>> float(out.loss.item()) >= 0.0
True
The representation a downstream task reads is the target encoder's:
>>> model.encode(lucid.rand(2, 4, 3, 32, 32)).shape
(2, 24)
notes:
Reference: Bardes, Adrien, et al., *"Revisiting Feature Prediction for
Learning Visual Representations from Video"*, [arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471), 2024,
Sections 3.1–3.3.

Clips are `(B, T, C, H, W)` with `T = config.num_frames`.  Call
`update_target` after each optimiser step, with the value
`momentum` gives.

The target features are layer-normalised without affine terms before
any block is taken from them — that is in the released code and not
in the paper, and it is the usual way a reimplementation fails.

parameters.name: pretrained
parameters.description: Not redistributed; `True` raises.

parameters.name: **overrides
parameters.description: Optional `VJEPAConfig` field overrides.

returns.description: The pretraining networks, an attentive pooler and a classifier.

notes:
Reference: Bardes et al., [arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471), Section 4.3.  `num_classes`
defaults to 400, Kinetics-400's count.

extended:
Bardes et al., 2024 ([arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471)).  A clip is cut into tubelets, two
collections of blocks hide most of them through the whole depth of the
clip, and a predictor says what an averaged copy of the encoder would
report about what is hidden.  The image version is
`lucid.models.vision.ijepa`; the transformer they share is in
`vision/_common`.
citation: Bardes, Adrien, et al. "Revisiting Feature Prediction for Learning Visual Representations from Video." [arXiv:2404.08471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08471), 2024.
theory:
V-JEPA learns from video by predicting *features* of what it cannot
see.  A clip of $T$ frames becomes $T/2 \times H/16 \times W/16$ tubelet tokens; a mask hides most of them; the encoder
$f_\theta$ reads what is left, and a predictor $g_\phi$
must produce the output of an exponentially averaged encoder
$f_{\bar\theta}$ at the hidden positions:



$$
\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{k=1}^{M}
\bigl\| g_\phi\bigl(f_\theta(x_{\text{context}}),\, p_k\bigr)
- \mathrm{sg}\bigl[f_{\bar\theta}(x)\bigr]_k \bigr\|_1 .
$$

**Two mask collections, not one.**  Eight blocks covering 15% of the
frame each, and two covering 70%, both running the full depth of the
clip in time.  Their union hides about 90% of the tokens.  A mask
that leaves a tube visible through time makes the task trivial ---
the answer is in the next frame --- so both collections extend
through it, and the model is asked the two questions at once, with a
learned mask token of its own for each.

**The target encoder sees everything; the context encoder does not.**
Masking here removes tokens rather than attending around them, so the
context encoder's sequence is genuinely shorter, while the averaged
encoder reads the whole clip and its output is normalised before any
block is taken from it.  No gradient flows into it at all.

**Prediction in feature space is what makes the video tractable.**
A generative video objective must settle every detail that differs
between plausible continuations; this one may drop whatever the
averaged encoder has already learned to drop.  Frozen, with an
attentive probe on top, the result reaches 82.0% on Kinetics-400 and
71.4% on Something-Something-v2 --- the latter being the benchmark
that punishes models which only recognise appearance.
